summary.text: A natural satellite, colloquially called a moon, is an astronomical body that orbits a planet, dwarf planet, or small Solar System body.
Moons on close, circular orbits are thought to have formed with their planet, while those on distant, tilted or backward orbits are thought to be captured asteroids.
Most regular moons in the Solar System are tidally locked, so the same side of the moon always faces its planet.

items.prompt: Astronomers spot a small moon circling a planet from far away, on a steeply tilted, backward path. Where did it most likely come from?

options.label: Leftover material from the disc that built its planet
A crash between two huge objects early in history
An asteroid that was captured and perhaps broken up
A chunk blasted off the planet by its own volcanoes

items.explain: Distant, inclined or retrograde orbits mark irregular satellites, which are thought to be captured asteroids. Moons formed with their planet sit close on circular orbits.

items.prompt: A camera in orbit around a planet photographs one of its typical regular moons every night for a year. What do the pictures show?

options.label: Each side of the moon in turn, over several weeks
A different side every night as it spins faster
Only the far side, since the near side is in shadow
The same side of the moon facing the planet each time

items.explain: Most regular moons are tidally locked, so the same side always faces their planet.

items.prompt: Why does a regular moon end up showing the same face to its planet?

options.label: Tidal forces from the planet drain its energy and slow its rotation
The planet's magnetic field pins one side in place for good
It stopped spinning the moment the planet captured it
Sunlight pushes on one side until it stops turning around

items.explain: Tides raised by the planet cost the moon energy and slow its rotation, which leaves the same side facing the planet.

items.prompt: A writer needs one term that cannot be mistaken for Earth's own Moon, for other planets' moons, or for spacecraft. Which term works?

options.label: Artificial moon
Satellite, used alone
Natural satellite
The capital-M Moon

items.explain: Satellite alone became linked with artificial objects, so natural satellite is used when both confusions must be avoided.

items.prompt: Triton is large and sits in a close, circular orbit, yet it moves backward around its planet. What is the best explanation?

options.label: It formed from the same disc as its planet
It is thought to be a captured dwarf planet
It formed from a clash of two large objects
It is a small companion at a trojan point

items.explain: A backward motion does not fit a moon formed with its planet, so Triton is thought to have been captured.

paragraphs.heading: What counts as a moon
paragraphs.text: A natural satellite is a body in space that orbits a planet, a dwarf planet or a small Solar System body, and sometimes even another satellite. In everyday speech these are called moons, after Earth's own Moon. English writes Moon with a capital M for Earth's satellite and moon in lowercase for the general kind.

paragraphs.heading: How many there are
paragraphs.text: Six planets in the Solar System have satellite systems, holding 456 natural satellites with confirmed orbits between them. Seven bodies that astronomers usually count as dwarf planets, among them Pluto and Eris, have moons too. Counting those seven, 652 minor planets are known or suspected to have satellites.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word came from
paragraphs.text: When Galileo found the Galilean satellites of Jupiter in 1610, he called them planets. That same year Johannes Kepler called them satellites, from the Latin satelles, meaning a guard or companion, since they travel along with their planet. Satellite became the normal word until the launch of Sputnik in 1957 tied it to machines in space. After that shift, moon came back into favour and is now used as an equal of natural satellite, even in scientific papers.

paragraphs.heading: Fuzzy edges
paragraphs.text: There is no agreed smallest size for a moon. Bodies around a kilometer wide that orbit a planet have been counted as moons, while far smaller objects in Saturn's rings, and small moons of asteroids such as Dactyl, have been called moonlets. The upper limit is vague too. Some authors call Pluto and Charon a double dwarf planet, partly because the barycentre of the pair lies above the surface of Pluto. For every planetary moon in the Solar System, the barycentre sits inside the planet.

paragraphs.heading: Regular and irregular moons
paragraphs.text: Regular satellites travel close to their planet on prograde, circular orbits that are not tilted, and they are thought to have formed from the same part of the disk that made the planet. Irregular satellites, often on distant, tilted, eccentric or retrograde orbits, are thought to be captured asteroids, perhaps broken up further by collisions. Most of the big moons are regular, and most of the small ones are irregular. Triton is an odd case: it is large and on a close, circular orbit, yet it moves retrograde and is thought to be a captured dwarf planet.

paragraphs.heading: Born from collisions
paragraphs.text: The Moon and Pluto's moons are thought to have formed another way, from a crash between two large bodies early in the Solar System's history. Material thrown into orbit by such a crash is predicted to gather again into one or more moons. Moons of asteroids are thought to form this way often.

paragraphs.heading: Same face forward
paragraphs.text: Most regular moons in the Solar System are tidally locked, which means the same side always faces their planet. This happens because tidal forces from the planet drain energy from the moon and slow its rotation. There are exceptions: Saturn's moon Hyperion tumbles chaotically under the pull of Titan.

paragraphs.heading: Odd companions
paragraphs.text: Saturn's moons Tethys and Dione each share their orbit with two small companions, one sixty degrees ahead and one sixty degrees behind. These are called trojan moons: Telesto and Calypso go with Tethys, and Helene and Polydeuces go with Dione. Some captures do not last, and simulations suggest temporary satellites should be common. One example, 2006 RH120, circled Earth as a temporary satellite for nine months across 2006 and 2007.
